passages.t: Amaziah, and a law that spared the children
passages.happening:
In the second year of Jehoash of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash becomes king of Judah at twenty-five and reigns twenty-nine years in Jerusalem (verses 1-2). ‘And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, but not as his father David had done’ (verse 3). The high places remain (verse 4).

Once the kingdom is firmly his, he executes the servants who had murdered his father (verse 5). But he does not put their sons to death. He follows the Book of the Law of Moses, where the LORD commanded, “Fathers must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin” (verse 6). He defeats ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and takes Sela (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Amaziah ruled Judah about 796 to 767 BC, though his years may overlap with his son's. His verdict is carefully graded: right in the LORD's eyes, but not like David, and the high places stay. The high places, bamah, were local hilltop shrines. Some served other gods, and many were used in the LORD's name but outside the one place Deuteronomy appointed for sacrifice. Kings faults even good kings for leaving them.

His restraint in verse 6 was striking in its world. When a new king took power after an assassination, it was common to wipe out the killers' whole families and so remove any future avengers. Amaziah instead obeys the law of Moses, and the narrator quotes it. The law was meant to shape a king's policy, not only the temple's worship. It limits the power of kings and protects the innocent, even when revenge would be convenient.
passages.later: The law in Deuteronomy says, ‘each is to die for his own sin’ (Deuteronomy 24:16), and Ezekiel later preached the same: ‘A son will not bear the iniquity of his father’ (Ezekiel 18:20).
passages.asks: Amaziah let the law of God restrain his revenge. Ask where God's word has held you back from paying someone back in full. And ask whether you would let it, if the person deserved it.

passages.happening:
Amaziah sends a challenge to Jehoash king of Israel: “Come, let us meet face to face” (verse 8). Jehoash answers with a fable. A thistle in Lebanon asked a cedar to give its daughter in marriage to its son, and a wild animal came by and trampled the thistle (verse 9). ‘You have indeed defeated Edom, and your heart has become proud. Glory in that and stay at home’ (verse 10).

Amaziah will not listen. The two kings meet at Beth-shemesh in Judah, and Judah is routed (verses 11-12). Jehoash captures Amaziah, goes up to Jerusalem, breaks down four hundred cubits of the wall, and carries off the gold and silver of the temple and palace, with hostages, to Samaria (verses 13-14).

Jehoash dies, and Amaziah outlives him by fifteen years (verses 15-17). Then conspirators plot against Amaziah in Jerusalem. He flees to Lachish, and they kill him there. He is buried in the City of David, and the people of Judah make his sixteen-year-old son Azariah king (verses 19-21). Azariah rebuilds Elath and restores it to Judah (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Judah's king overreaches and is humbled by his northern neighbor, a reminder that the split begun under Rehoboam still breaks out into open war. A call to meet face to face could sound like an invitation to talk, but Jehoash hears it as a challenge to battle.

His answer is a fable, a short story about plants or animals with a moral, a form well known in the ancient world; Jotham's fable of the trees in Judges is another. The thistle, choach, is a lowly prickly weed set against the cedar, the grandest tree of Lebanon. The word tells Amaziah exactly how Jehoash ranks Judah beside Israel. The keynote of the scene is pride; the Hebrew in verse 10 speaks of the heart lifted up. A victory God had given became the ground of arrogance, and arrogance led a nation into disaster.

Four hundred cubits is about 180 meters, or 600 feet, of wall. Breaking it down was a deliberate humiliation that left the capital exposed, and the hostages secured Judah's good behavior.
passages.later: Proverbs says, ‘Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall’ (Proverbs 16:18). Jotham's fable begins, ‘One day the trees set out to anoint a king for themselves’ (Judges 9:8).
passages.asks: Amaziah kept God's law in a hard moment and then was undone by pride after a victory. Ask why success can be more dangerous to faith than failure. And ask how you hear a hard truth when it comes from someone who does not wish you well.

passages.t: Jeroboam II, and a mercy he did not earn
passages.happening:
In the fifteenth year of Amaziah, Jeroboam son of Jehoash becomes king of Israel and reigns forty-one years in Samaria (verse 23). He does evil and keeps the sins of the first Jeroboam (verse 24).

‘This Jeroboam restored the boundary of Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word that the LORD, the God of Israel, had spoken through His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher’ (verse 25). ‘For the LORD saw that the affliction of the Israelites, both slave and free, was very bitter. There was no one to help Israel’ (verse 26). The LORD had not said he would blot out Israel's name, so he saved them by Jeroboam's hand (verse 27). Jeroboam dies, and his son Zechariah reigns (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Jeroboam II ruled about 793 to 753 BC, probably at first beside his father. His expansion was possible because Assyrian campaigns had weakened Aram-Damascus, while Assyria itself went through a time of weakness in the first half of the eighth century and did not press west in force. For a generation the small kingdoms had room to grow.

The narrator gives one of Israel's longest and most successful reigns only a few verses and explains it entirely as mercy. Verse 26 echoes the song of Moses, where the LORD sees that his people's strength is gone and no one is left, slave or free. The verb blot out, machah, means to wipe clean, as one wipes a dish. Its careful wording here means not yet, and the same verb comes back in 21:13, when the LORD says he will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish.

Amos and Hosea both date their preaching to Jeroboam's reign, and their books show the view from below: luxury for the wealthy, oppression of the poor and worship that went through the motions. Archaeology fits a time of plenty. The Samaria ostraca, inked potsherds recording shipments of wine and oil to the capital, are usually dated to the early eighth century. A fine seal found at Megiddo, belonging to Shema, servant of Jeroboam, is often, though not always, assigned to this king. The Jonah of verse 25 is the prophet whose book tells of his mission to Nineveh. A reader who knows what comes next, six kings in about thirty years and then the fall of Samaria, feels how thin the ice was under this prosperity.
passages.later: Amos, preaching in these years, said to the wealthy of Samaria, ‘You lie on beds inlaid with ivory, and lounge upon your couches’ (Amos 6:4). The book of Jonah begins, ‘Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai’ (Jonah 1:1), and Jesus spoke of ‘the sign of the prophet Jonah’ (Matthew 12:39).
passages.hard:
Why did God give Jeroboam II success when the text says he did evil?

Kings does not hide the tension. Jeroboam keeps the calf shrines at Bethel and Dan, and yet his reign brings Israel its widest borders in generations, in fulfillment of a prophet's word. The narrator's explanation is that the success was not a reward for Jeroboam. It was mercy for a suffering people, and it came because God had not yet decreed Israel's end.

Readers have drawn two lessons from this. One is that prosperity is not proof of God's approval. Amos, preaching in these same years, saw the wealth of Samaria as a sign of injustice and announced judgment on it. The other is that God's patience has a purpose. The years of Jeroboam were a space for repentance, and the prophets of the time called the nation to use it. When it did not, the prosperity ended within a generation.
passages.asks: God rescued Israel through a king who did evil. Ask what it means that God's kindness to you is not proof that everything in your life has his approval. And ask what you are doing with a season of plenty.
